description:
What this shows: Ledger data exchange and object-fetch traffic between this node and its peers: ledger sync, tree-node retrieval, and transaction-set exchange.
Use it to: See how much ledger data the node is pulling or serving and spot catch-up activity.

panels.title: Ledger Data — Ledger
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Inbound bytes for ledger-data message categories, split into aggregate get/share plus the transaction-set, transaction-node, and account-state-node sub-types the node receives from peers.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-category inbound byte rate per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Normally low and flat once synced. Account-state-node traffic dominates during state sync; transaction-set-candidate traffic dominates during consensus catch-up.*

###### Healthy range:
*workload-dependent; low and steady on a synced node.*

###### Watch for:
*Sustained high account-state or tx-node inbound bytes on a node that should be caught up (repeated re-sync, missing history), or a single peer driving all traffic.*

###### Source:
[OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:
`OverlayImpl ctor (TrafficGauges)`

panels.title: GetObject — Ledger
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Inbound bytes for object-fetch traffic broken down by object type: ledger headers, individual transactions, transaction-tree nodes, and state-tree nodes.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-type inbound byte rate per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Small during steady state; grows when the node fetches missing tree nodes.*

###### Healthy range:
*workload-dependent; low when synced.*

###### Watch for:
*A large share on state/tx nodes for long periods (persistent gap-filling), meaning the node keeps catching up.*

###### Source:
[OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:

panels.title: GetObject Messages — Ledger
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Count of individual object-fetch request/response messages per object type.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-type inbound message rate per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Many messages with few bytes means small piecemeal fetches; few messages with many bytes means large batch transfers.*

###### Healthy range:
*workload-dependent.*

###### Watch for:
*High message counts with tiny payloads sustained over time (inefficient per-node fetching).*

###### Source:
[OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:

panels.title: GetObject — Specials
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Aggregate object-fetch inbound bytes plus special buckets: content-addressed storage fetches, bulk fetch-pack downloads used during catch-up, and bulk transaction fetches.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-category inbound byte rate per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Fetch-pack rises sharply while catching up a range of ledgers; near zero when fully synced.*

###### Healthy range:
*workload-dependent; low when synced.*

###### Watch for:
*Continuous fetch-pack traffic (node never fully catches up) or unexpectedly high content-store volume.*

###### Source:
[OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:
`OverlayImpl ctor (TrafficGauges)`

panels.title: Overlay Traffic Heatmap (All Categories, Bytes In)
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*All overlay traffic categories ranked by inbound bytes, giving an at-a-glance view of which message types consume the most receive bandwidth.*

###### How it's computed:
*Top categories by latest inbound byte value across all traffic categories. Each bar is labelled with its traffic category followed by the node identity; the shared `_bytes_in` suffix is dropped from the category name because the panel already reports inbound bytes.*

###### Reading it:
*The longest bars are the biggest bandwidth consumers; on a synced node transactions, proposals, and validations usually lead.*

###### Healthy range:
*workload-dependent.*

###### Watch for:
*A single ledger-data or fetch category dominating (ongoing sync) or an unexpected category topping the list.*

###### Source:
[OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:
`OverlayImpl ctor (TrafficGauges)`

panels.title: Sync State
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Current server operating state as a numeric code: 0 disconnected, 1 connected, 2 syncing, 3 tracking, 4 full. A healthy synced node sits at 4.*

###### How it's computed:
*state_tracking{metric="state_value"} (gauge). Companion time_in_current_state_seconds shows how long it has been stuck there.*

###### Reading it:
*Flat at 4 = full/healthy. Dropping to 1-2 and staying = the node fell out of sync and is re-acquiring (the primary red flag this row explains).*

###### Healthy range:
*4 (full), briefly 2-3 right after restart.*

###### Watch for:
*A node stuck below 4 for more than a few minutes, or oscillating - read the lower panels for the cause.*

###### Source:
[app/misc/NetworkOPs.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/app/misc/NetworkOPs.cpp)

###### Function:
`NetworkOPsImp::setMode`

panels.title: Validated Ledger Age
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Seconds since this node last had a freshly validated ledger. The single clearest 'am I keeping up with the network' signal.*

###### How it's computed:
*ledgermaster_validated_ledger_age gauge (seconds), per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Should hover at the network close interval (~3-5s). A rising sawtooth or a high plateau means the node is falling behind or not validating.*

###### Healthy range:
*<= ~6s on a synced node.*

###### Watch for:
*Sustained climb above ~15s, or a monotonic ramp = the node is not keeping up; correlate with job-queue wait and NuDB read latency below.*

###### Source:
[app/ledger/LedgerMaster.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/app/ledger/detail/LedgerMaster.cpp)

###### Function:
`LedgerMaster::getValidatedLedgerAge`

panels.title: Ledger Close Rate
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Rate at which the node closes ledgers, versus the ~0.25/s network cadence. A throughput deficit means it is not advancing in step with the network.*

###### How it's computed:
*rate(ledgers_closed_total[$__rate_interval]) per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Should track ~0.22-0.25 ledgers/s (one every ~4s). Near-zero while behind = stalled; a burst above network rate = catching up.*

###### Healthy range:
*~0.25/s steady on a synced node.*

###### Watch for:
*Near-zero close rate while Validated Ledger Age climbs = hard stall (e.g. genesis-flapping or disk-bound acquisition).*

###### Source:
[app/ledger/LedgerMaster.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/app/ledger/detail/LedgerMaster.cpp)

###### Function:
`LedgerMaster::closeLedger`

panels.title: Job Queue Wait p95 By Type
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*95th-percentile time a job waits in the queue before a worker thread picks it up, for the sync-critical job types. This is the metric form of the 'ProcessLData wait: NNNNms' warnings in the debug log.*

###### How it's computed:
*histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(jobq_<type>_q_milliseconds_bucket[$__rate_interval])) for ledgerdata, acceptledger, fetchtxndata, transaction, advanceledger, ledgerrequest.*

###### Reading it:
*Queue wait should be single-digit to low-tens of ms. High ledgerdata/fetchtxndata wait = the node cannot process inbound ledger data fast enough.*

###### Healthy range:
*< ~50ms p95 per type on a healthy node.*

###### Watch for:
*ledgerdata or fetchtxndata q-wait spiking to seconds = worker threads are blocked (usually on NuDB reads - see the cause tier).*

###### Source:
[core/JobQueue.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/core/detail/JobQueue.cpp)

###### Function:
`JobQueue::getJson (per-type queue timing)`

panels.title: NuDB Read Latency
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Average nodestore (NuDB) read latency: how long each on-disk object read takes. The direct disk-layer cost that backs up the job queue.*

###### How it's computed:
*rate(nodestore_state{metric="node_reads_duration_us"}[$__rate_interval]) / rate(nodestore_state{metric="node_reads_total"}[$__rate_interval]), in us.*

###### Reading it:
*Low single-digit us when the OS page cache is warm; tens-to-hundreds of us when reads hit the disk. Rises sharply during cold-cache catch-up.*

###### Healthy range:
*< ~10us/read warm; higher is expected briefly after a wipe/restart.*

###### Watch for:
*Sustained high us/read together with low cache hit % (below) = disk-bound reads are the bottleneck; check EBS IOPS / io scheduler latency.*

###### Source:
[nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp)

###### Function:
`NuDB backend read path`

targets.expr: label_replace(label_join(label_replace(sum by (service_instance_id, xrpl_branch, xrpl_node_role) (rate(nodestore_state{service_instance_id=~"$node", deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment", xrpl_network_type=~"$xrpl_network_type", service_name=~"$service_name", xrpl_work_item=~"$xrpl_work_item", xrpl_branch=~"$xrpl_branch", xrpl_node_role=~"$xrpl_node_role", metric="node_reads_duration_us"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (service_instance_id, xrpl_branch, xrpl_node_role) (rate(nodestore_state{service_instance_id=~"$node", deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment", xrpl_network_type=~"$xrpl_network_type", service_name=~"$service_name", xrpl_work_item=~"$xrpl_work_item", xrpl_branch=~"$xrpl_branch", xrpl_node_role=~"$xrpl_node_role", metric="node_reads_total"}[$__rate_interval])), 1), "series", "NuDB us/read", "", ""), "xrpl_ident", ", ", "service_instance_id", "xrpl_branch", "xrpl_work_item"), "xrpl_ident", "[$1]", "xrpl_ident", "(?:, )*(.*[^, ])(?:, )*")

panels.title: I/O Scheduler Latency p95
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*95th-percentile latency of the node's internal I/O service queue - the async task scheduler that dispatches network and disk callbacks.*

###### How it's computed:
*histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(ios_latency_milliseconds_bucket[$__rate_interval])).*

###### Reading it:
*Low and flat when the event loop is responsive. Rising p95 means callbacks are queuing behind long-running work (often blocking disk reads).*

###### Healthy range:
*< ~10ms p95.*

###### Watch for:
*p95 climbing into hundreds of ms = the I/O service is saturated; the node cannot service network/disk events promptly, stalling sync.*

###### Source:
[core/impl/Workers.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/core/detail/Workers.cpp)

###### Function:
`io_service latency histogram`

targets.expr: label_replace(label_join(label_replace(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, service_instance_id, xrpl_branch, xrpl_node_role) (rate(ios_latency_milliseconds_bucket{service_instance_id=~"$node", deployment_environment=~"$deployment_environment", xrpl_network_type=~"$xrpl_network_type", service_name=~"$service_name", xrpl_work_item=~"$xrpl_work_item", xrpl_branch=~"$xrpl_branch", xrpl_node_role=~"$xrpl_node_role"}[$__rate_interval]))), "series", "IO Service p95", "", ""), "xrpl_ident", ", ", "service_instance_id", "xrpl_branch", "xrpl_work_item"), "xrpl_ident", "[$1]", "xrpl_ident", "(?:, )*(.*[^, ])(?:, )*")

panels.title: NuDB Cache Hit Ratio
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Fraction of nodestore reads served from cache rather than disk. A cold cache (fresh NuDB after a wipe) forces almost every read to disk - the root cause of high read latency during catch-up.*

###### How it's computed:
*rate(nodestore_state{metric="node_reads_hit"}[$__rate_interval]) / rate(nodestore_state{metric="node_reads_total"}[$__rate_interval]).*

###### Reading it:
*Near 1.0 (100%) on a warm node. Near 0 right after a wipe/restart, climbing as the working set warms.*

###### Healthy range:
*> ~0.9 warm; near 0 briefly after a cold start.*

###### Watch for:
*Persistently low hit ratio on a node that should be warm = working set does not fit cache, or continuous re-acquisition churning the cache.*

###### Source:
[nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp)

###### Function:
`TaggedCache hit accounting`

panels.title: NuDB Read Pressure
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Nodestore read throughput and backlog: reads per second, the pending read queue depth, and how many read threads are active. Shows disk saturation depth.*

###### How it's computed:
*rate(node_reads_total), and gauges read_queue / read_threads_running from nodestore_state.*

###### Reading it:
*reads/s spikes during catch-up. A growing read_queue with all read threads busy = disk cannot keep up with demand.*

###### Healthy range:
*read_queue ~0 and reads/s low on a warm synced node.*

###### Watch for:
*read_queue climbing while read_threads_running is pinned at read_threads_total = disk-bound; the IOPS ceiling is the limiter.*

###### Source:
[nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/nodestore/backend/NuDBFactory.cpp)

###### Function:
`NuDB read scheduler`

panels.title: Job Queue Depth
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Total number of jobs currently queued across the JobQueue. A backlog means work is arriving faster than worker threads can drain it.*

###### How it's computed:
*jobq_job_count gauge (total queued jobs), per node.*

###### Reading it:
*Near 0 when keeping up. Sustained positive depth = the node is overloaded or blocked on a downstream resource (usually disk reads).*

###### Healthy range:
*~0 on a healthy node.*

###### Watch for:
*Depth climbing in step with Validated Ledger Age = the queue backlog is why the node is falling behind.*

###### Source:
[core/JobQueue.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/core/detail/JobQueue.cpp)

###### Function:
`JobQueue::getJobCountTotal`

panels.title: Load Factor & Peers
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Server load factor (fee/throttle multiplier; 1 = unloaded) alongside active inbound/outbound peer counts. Rules out overload and insufficient fetch sources as causes.*

###### How it's computed:
*load_factor_metrics{metric="load_factor"}, and peer_finder_active_inbound_peers / _outbound_peers gauges.*

###### Reading it:
*load_factor at 1 = no local overload. Outbound peers should be healthy (~10+); too few peers limits how fast the node can fetch ledger data.*

###### Healthy range:
*load_factor = 1; outbound peers >= ~8.*

###### Watch for:
*load_factor > 1 = local overload throttling; very low peer count = not enough sources to acquire history from (a distinct sync bottleneck).*

###### Source:
[overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/overlay/detail/OverlayImpl.cpp)

###### Function:
`OverlayImpl load / PeerFinder counts`
